CHI Internship: SAR Systems Integration Practicum, Technical Report 04

**CTRL-VIDEO-01-T01: TD Output to QLab Camera Cue over NDI**

Experiment series: CTRL-VIDEO-01  
Test: 01  
Date: 2026-10-08  
Status: Preview passed; final projector path and latency not validated

*Closing the Loop Between Show Control and Media*

**Gabriel A. Aguilar**  
Center for Holistic Integration (CHI), Self-Aware Room (SAR)  
CUNY New York City College of Technology, Brooklyn, NY

October 8, 2026

**Abstract**

The first three tests taught QLab and TouchDesigner to exchange commands; Test 04 asks them to share a picture. This report documents the routing of TouchDesigner’s live video output into a QLab Camera cue using NDI, a protocol for sending video over an ordinary network, across the same direct Ethernet cable used in Tests 01 through 03\. An NDI Out TOP in TouchDesigner published the output of the clip-switching network, and QLab received it as a video input patch at 1280 by 720 from 192.168.10.20. Because the stream carries whatever TouchDesigner is showing, a single GO now travels a full loop: QLab sends a clip index, TouchDesigner switches the clip, the new image returns to QLab as video, and the acknowledgment from Test 03 renames the ACK cue. No additional hardware was required. The main issue was that the Camera cue first played full screen on the main display, which was resolved for testing by previewing the feed in QLab’s Monitor window.

***Keywords:** NDI, Video over IP, QLab Camera Cue, TouchDesigner, Show Control, Self-Aware Room*

# **1\. Introduction**

Tests 01 through 03 established a working conversation between QLab and TouchDesigner: QLab can tell TouchDesigner which clip to show, and TouchDesigner can answer back (Aguilar, 2026a, 2026b, 2026c). Words, however, are only half of a performance. For the Self-Aware Room, the media that TouchDesigner generates also needs to reach QLab, so that the show-control system can place it, layer it, and cue it alongside everything else in the room.

The obvious tool on a Mac would be Syphon, which shares video between applications; however, Syphon only works between programs on the same computer, and our TouchDesigner machine is a Windows PC. I chose NDI instead. QLab 5 Camera cues accept any NDI source on the Mac’s local network (Figure 53, n.d.), and TouchDesigner includes an NDI Out TOP, so the stream can ride the existing Ethernet link without a capture card. The success criteria were:

1. TouchDesigner publishes its output as an NDI source over the direct Ethernet link.

2. QLab detects that source and receives a live image in a Camera cue.

3. Clip changes made through the OSC cues from Tests 01 through 03 appear in QLab’s video feed.

4. The OSC handshake continues to work while video shares the same cable.

# **2\. Materials and Methods**

## ***2.1 Equipment, Software and Network***

The equipment, software, and network were unchanged from the earlier tests (Table 1). The NDI stream is sent from the TouchDesigner machine at 192.168.10.20, so it travels on the same cable as the OSC traffic.

**Table 1\.** *Network addressing, unchanged across Tests 01 through 03\.*

| Setting | QLab machine (macOS) | TouchDesigner machine |
| :---- | :---- | :---- |
| Ethernet IP | 192.168.10.10 | 192.168.10.20 |
| Subnet mask | 255.255.255.0 | 255.255.255.0 |
| Router / gateway | blank | blank |
| Wi-Fi address | 10.2.215.89 (campus) | campus network |
| OSC listening port | 53000 (QLab default) | 7000 (OSC In CHOP and DAT) |

## ***2.2 TouchDesigner Configuration***

I added an NDI Out TOP named SAR\_TD\_Out and wired it to null1, the same final output that already feeds the Window COMP. That way the NDI stream always matches whatever clip the Switch TOP has selected (Figure 1; Table 2).

![The NDI Out TOP SAR\_TD\_Out, wired in parallel with window1 from null1, and its parameters: Active on, Source Name “TouchDesigner,” 60 FPS, 8-bit output, alpha off.][image1]

**Figure 1\.** *The NDI Out TOP SAR\_TD\_Out, wired in parallel with window1 from null1, and its parameters: Active on, Source Name “TouchDesigner,” 60 FPS, 8-bit output, alpha off.*

**Table 2\.** *NDI Out TOP parameters.*

| Parameter | Value |
| :---- | :---- |
| Operator name | SAR\_TD\_Out |
| Input | null1 (final output of the clip-switching network) |
| Active | On |
| Source Name | TouchDesigner |
| FPS | 60 |
| Low-Performance Behavior | Stall Main Thread |
| Output Pixel Format | 8-bit |
| Include Alpha | Off |

## ***2.3 QLab Configuration***

On the QLab side, the stream first had to become a video input patch. Under Workspace Settings, Video, Video Inputs, I created Patch 2 and chose the device QLab listed as “AQUILAPC (TouchDesigner)”; that name combines the Windows machine’s name with the Source Name set in TouchDesigner. QLab reported the source at 192.168.10.20:5961 with a resolution of 1280 by 720 (Figure 2).

I then configured the Camera cue left over from Test 01, renamed it “TD CAMERA,” and in its I/O tab set Video Input to Patch 2\. Because the source is NDI, QLab takes audio from the stream itself, and the Audio Input field reads “No audio.”

![Workspace Settings, Video, Video Inputs: Patch 2 uses the NDI source AQUILAPC (TouchDesigner) at 192.168.10.20:5961, 1280 by 720. Below, the I/O tab of the TD CAMERA cue with Video Input set to Patch 2.][image2]

**Figure 2\.** *Workspace Settings, Video, Video Inputs: Patch 2 uses the NDI source AQUILAPC (TouchDesigner) at 192.168.10.20:5961, 1280 by 720\. Below, the I/O tab of the TD CAMERA cue with Video Input set to Patch 2\.*

**Table 3\.** *QLab settings for Test 04\.*

| Setting | Value |
| :---- | :---- |
| Video input patch | Patch 2, device AQUILAPC (TouchDesigner) |
| Reported source | 192.168.10.20:5961, 1280 by 720 |
| Camera cue | Cue 2, renamed TD CAMERA |
| Camera cue Video Input | Patch 2 \- AQUILAPC (TouchDesigner) |
| Camera cue Audio Input | No audio (NDI supplies its own) |

## ***2.4 Procedure***

1. Add and activate the NDI Out TOP in TouchDesigner.

2. Create a video input patch in QLab using the TouchDesigner NDI source, and assign it to the Camera cue.

3. Open the Monitor window for the input and confirm a live image.

4. Fire the clip cues from Test 01 and watch the image in QLab and the name of the ACK cue.

# **3\. Results**

The test passed. QLab found the TouchDesigner stream on its own, and the Monitor window showed a live image that followed the clip cues (Figure 3). In the moment captured, the most recent GO had sent index 1: QLab’s Monitor window shows clip 1 arriving over NDI, and the ACK cue reads “TD got clip 1,” while the playhead has moved on to the index 2 cue. That single frame holds the entire loop: a command out, a clip change, a picture back, and an acknowledgment.

![QLab with the Monitor Input window for Patch 2 (right) showing clip 1 received from TouchDesigner over NDI. In the cue list, the ACK cue reads “TD got clip 1” and the TD CAMERA cue sits at cue 2.][image3]

**Figure 3\.** *QLab with the Monitor Input window for Patch 2 (right) showing clip 1 received from TouchDesigner over NDI. In the cue list, the ACK cue reads “TD got clip 1” and the TD CAMERA cue sits at cue 2\.*

**Table 4\.** *Results against the success criteria.*

| Check | Result |
| :---- | :---- |
| TouchDesigner publishes an NDI source over Ethernet | Pass (192.168.10.20:5961) |
| QLab detects the source and shows a live image | Pass (1280 by 720\) |
| Clip changes from OSC cues appear in QLab’s feed | Pass |
| OSC handshake still works with video on the same cable | Pass (ACK updated) |
| Frame rate received and latency | Not measured |

Two details are worth noting. First, the source address shows that the video travelled over the Ethernet link rather than campus Wi-Fi. Second, QLab displayed the message “QLab does not currently have permission to access video inputs” in its Video Inputs settings, yet the NDI feed still played; the macOS camera permission appears to govern physical cameras such as the built-in FaceTime camera, not network sources.

# **4\. Discussion**

## ***4.1 Issues Encountered and Resolutions***

This was the smoothest test so far; the only real snag concerned where QLab chose to show the picture (Table 5).

**Table 5\.** *Issues encountered during Test 04\.*

| Issue | Cause | Resolution |
| :---- | :---- | :---- |
| The Camera cue played full screen on the main display | The cue’s stage is routed to a full display | Previewed the feed in QLab’s Monitor window; a separate preview stage routed to the laptop screen is recommended for future testing |
| “QLab does not currently have permission to access video inputs” | macOS camera permission for QLab is off | No action needed for NDI; enable it under Privacy & Security, Camera if a physical camera is used |
| Generic NDI source name | Source Name left at the default “TouchDesigner” | Open item: rename the source to identify the SAR stream, such as SAR\_TD\_Out |

## ***4.2 Limitations***

* I did not measure latency between the TouchDesigner output and QLab’s image; with video involved, this number matters more than in any earlier test.

* The frame rate QLab actually received was not recorded; TouchDesigner was set to 60 FPS.

* The stream ran at 1280 by 720; full HD or higher may behave differently on the same link.

* Network load from the video stream was not measured, nor was its effect on OSC timing beyond the ACK continuing to update.

* The feed was confirmed in the Monitor window; final output to a projector through a dedicated stage was not tested.

## ***4.3 Implications for the SAR Standard***

Most importantly, this test shows that one Ethernet cable can carry both control and media between the two systems: commands, acknowledgments, and video together. That simplifies the room considerably, since no capture hardware is needed between TouchDesigner and QLab. The SAR standard should still name NDI sources clearly, reserve a preview stage for testing, and confirm that every machine’s network adapter runs at gigabit speed before video is added to the link.

# **5\. Conclusion and Future Work**

In conclusion, TouchDesigner’s output can be brought into a QLab Camera cue over NDI on the existing direct Ethernet link, and the command, the media, and the acknowledgment now travel together. The room can now see what it shows. The open items are:

* Measure end-to-end latency, for example by filming both outputs with a frame counter visible.

* Record the received frame rate and test 1920 by 1080\.

* Rename the NDI source and create a dedicated preview stage.

* Route the TD CAMERA cue to a real output stage and confirm the image on the projector.

* Fold these checks into a Test 05 reliability suite with cable loss, restarts, and heartbeat messages.
